name: ATMEGA64M1-AU
title: ATmega16M1/32M1/64M1 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with CAN, LIN/UART and a power stage controller, 16 to 64 Kbytes Flash, 2.7 V to 5.5 V
summary: A family of 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers aimed at motor and automotive-network control: a CAN 2.0A/B controller with six message objects, a LIN 2.1/1.3 controller that doubles as an 8-bit UART, and a 12-bit power stage controller (PSC) that drives non-overlapping complementary PWM pairs with dead time. They run most of their 131 instructions in one clock, close to 1 MIPS per MHz, up to 16 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V and 8 MHz from 2.7 V. Analog parts are a 10-bit ADC with 11 single-ended inputs and three differential pairs with programmable gain, a 10-bit DAC, four comparators and a 100 uA current source. The members differ in memory: 16, 32 or 64 Kbytes of Flash, 512 bytes to 2 Kbytes of EEPROM and 1 to 4 Kbytes of SRAM. ATMEGA64M1-AU is the 64 Kbyte part in the 32-lead TQFP.
key_figures: 8-bit AVR, 32 x 8 working registers, up to 1 MIPS per MHz, 2-cycle multiplier
64 Kbytes Flash, 2 Kbytes EEPROM, 4 Kbytes SRAM

operation.text: An 8-bit AVR RISC core with 131 instructions, most of them single-cycle, 32 x 8 working registers, fully static operation and a 2-cycle on-chip multiplier, reaching up to 1 MIPS per MHz. Flash is in-system programmable with an optional boot section that has its own lock bits, so an on-chip boot program can reprogram the part with true read-while-write. Lock bits protect the Flash and EEPROM contents. Debug runs over the one-wire debugWIRE interface.

A CAN 2.0A/B controller holding six message objects, certified to ISO 16845; a LIN controller (versions 2.1 and 1.3) that can instead work as an 8-bit UART; a fast 12-bit power stage controller (PSC) whose complementary PWM outputs never overlap, with adjustable dead time, adjustable frequency and duty cycle, every PWM register updated at the same instant, and an automatic stop when an emergency input fires.

One 8-bit and one 16-bit timer/counter, each with its own prescaler, compare and capture; a master/slave SPI; a 10-bit ADC with internal reference and direct supply-voltage measurement; a 10-bit DAC that serves as a variable reference for the comparators and ADC; four analog comparators with variable threshold; a 100 uA +/-2% current source for LIN node identification; pin-change interrupt and wake-up; a watchdog with its own on-chip oscillator; an on-chip temperature sensor. System features: three low-power sleep modes (idle, ADC noise reduction, power-down), a power-on reset and a brown-out detector with selectable level, programming in the system through the SPI port, a high-precision crystal oscillator for CAN (16 MHz), an internal calibrated 8 MHz RC oscillator, and an on-chip PLL giving 32 MHz or 64 MHz for fast PWM and 16 MHz for the CPU. Operating voltage 2.7 V to 5.5 V, temperature -40 °C to +85 °C.

The six PSC outputs (PSCOUT0A, PSCOUT0B, PSCOUT1A, PSCOUT1B, PSCOUT2A, PSCOUT2B) exist on the ATmega32M1 and ATmega64M1 only. Engineering samples carry ACMPN3 on PE2 instead of PC4. The 32-lead TQFP and the 32-pad QFN share one pin numbering.

Each device carries 27 general-purpose I/O lines, 32 working registers, the PSC for motor power stages, an 8-bit and a 16-bit timer/counter (both with compare and PWM), a UART with LIN in hardware, a 10-bit ADC of 11 channels whose differential inputs have gain stages, a 10-bit DAC, a programmable watchdog with its own oscillator, an SPI port, on-chip debug and four software-selected power saving modes.

Idle stops the CPU while SRAM, timers, SPI, CAN, LIN/UART and interrupts keep running. Power-down keeps register contents but stops the oscillator and everything else until an interrupt or hardware reset. ADC Noise Reduction halts the CPU and every I/O module but the ADC, to keep switching noise off conversions. Standby keeps the crystal or resonator oscillator running while the rest sleeps, for a very fast start-up at low power.

The Flash can be rewritten without removing the part: through the SPI port, with a standard parallel programmer, or by a boot program running on the core, which may load the application through any interface. Code in the Boot Flash section keeps running while the Application section is written.

Ports B, C and D are 8-bit and Port E is 3-bit bidirectional I/O, each bit with its own selectable pull-up. The output buffers are symmetrical with high sink and source capability. An input pulled low externally sources current when its pull-up is on. All port pins go tri-state as soon as a reset is active, with or without a running clock.

operation.topic: Port E, reset and crystal pins
operation.text: PE0 serves as the reset input while RSTDISBL is unprogrammed; it resets the part, with or without a running clock, when held low beyond the minimum pulse length, and a shorter low pulse is not guaranteed to act. Programming RSTDISBL turns PE0 into an I/O pin with electrical characteristics of its own, unlike PE1 and PE2. Under the clock fuse settings PE1 can be the inverting oscillator amplifier's input, which also feeds the internal clock circuit, and PE2 that amplifier's output.

AVCC supplies the A/D converter, D/A converter and current source. It is connected to VCC even when the ADC and DAC are not used, and through a low-pass filter when the ADC is used. AREF is the analog reference pin of the A/D converter.
Qualification results project fewer than 1 ppm data retention failures: 20 years is the span at 85 °C, 100 years the span at 25 °C.

The core is a Harvard design, with separate buses and memories for program and data, and a one-stage pipeline: the next instruction is fetched while the current one executes, so an instruction completes every clock. The 32 x 8 register file is single-cycle: two operands are read, the ALU operates and the result is written back in one clock. Six registers pair up as the 16-bit pointers X, Y and Z for indirect data addressing; Z can also point into Flash for table look-ups.

operation.topic: Program flow, interrupts and I/O space
operation.text: Jump and call instructions reach the whole address space. Most instructions are one 16-bit word; each program address holds a 16- or 32-bit instruction. Flash is split into a Boot Program section and an Application section, each with its own lock bits; the SPM instruction that writes the Application section must run from the Boot section. Calls and interrupts push the return address onto a stack in SRAM, so the stack size is bounded only by SRAM; the reset routine must set SP before any call or interrupt. Every interrupt has its own vector, and a lower vector address means a higher priority. The I/O space has 64 addresses, reachable directly or as data space 0x20 - 0x5F; the extended I/O space 0x60 - 0xFF is reached only with ST/STS/STD and LD/LDS/LDD.

The ALU works in one clock between two registers or between a register and a constant, in three groups: arithmetic, logical and bit functions, with a signed/unsigned and fractional multiplier. The status register is updated after every ALU operation and is not saved or restored automatically on interrupt entry and return; software does that.

The register file supports one 8-bit operand with an 8-bit result, two 8-bit operands with an 8-bit result, two 8-bit operands with a 16-bit result, and one 16-bit operand with a 16-bit result. R0 to R31 also sit at data addresses 0x00 to 0x1F, so X, Y and Z can index any register. R26/R27 form X, R28/R29 Y and R30/R31 Z, each low byte first; they serve indirect addressing with fixed displacement, post-increment and pre-decrement.

The stack grows from higher to lower addresses and SP points to its top; a PUSH decrements SP. The program must set up the stack before calls are made or interrupts enabled. SP's initial value is the last address of internal SRAM and it must point above the start of SRAM. SP is two 8-bit I/O registers, SPL and SPH.
SPL/SPH sit at I/O offset 0x3D (data address 0x5D) and reset to 0x10FF, with bits SP12 to SP0 implemented.

The data bus is 8 bits wide, so a 16-bit register is reached through a temporary register in two byte accesses. Write the low byte first (it goes to the temporary register) and then the high byte (both bytes land in the same clock). Read the low byte first (the high byte is copied to the temporary register at the same moment) and then the high byte. An interrupt that touches the same 16-bit register between the two accesses corrupts the transfer, so interrupts can be disabled around it. Software can read and write the temporary registers directly.

The CPU clock clkCPU comes straight from the selected clock source with no internal division. Fetch and execute overlap, giving up to 1 MIPS per MHz, and a two-register ALU operation completes, result written back, in one cycle.

Each interrupt source and the reset have their own vector in program memory, and each interrupt has an enable bit that works together with the global interrupt enable bit I in SREG. Programming the boot lock bits BLB02 or BLB12 can disable interrupts depending on where the program counter is. The vectors sit at the lowest program addresses by default; RESET has the highest priority, then INT0. Setting IVSEL in MCUCR relocates the interrupt vectors to the beginning of the boot section, and programming the BOOTRST fuse relocates the reset vector there too.

On entering an interrupt, I is cleared, disabling further interrupts; software may set it again to allow nesting, and RETI sets it. Flag-type interrupts set a flag that hardware clears when the vector is taken, or software clears by writing a one; a flag set while the interrupt or I is disabled is remembered and served in priority order once enabled. Level-type interrupts trigger only while their condition lasts and may have no flag. After returning from an interrupt, the core always executes one more main-program instruction before serving a pending interrupt. CLI takes effect at once, even against an interrupt arriving in the same cycle; after SEI the next instruction runs before any pending interrupt.

Response takes at least four clock cycles, during which the program counter is pushed; the vector, normally a jump, then takes three cycles. A multi-cycle instruction in progress completes first. Waking from sleep adds four cycles on top of the start-up time of the sleep mode. A return from interrupt takes four cycles: the two-byte PC is popped, SP rises by two and I is set.

16, 32 or 64 Kbytes of in-system reprogrammable Flash, organized in 16-bit words because every instruction is 16 or 32 bits wide, endurance at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. Constant tables can sit anywhere in program memory and are read with LPM.

The data space begins with the 32-register file, then 64 standard I/O locations, then 160 extended I/O locations, then 1, 2 or 4 Kbytes of internal SRAM from 0x0100. The extended I/O space 0x60 - 0xFF is reached only with ST/STS/STD and LD/LDS/LDD. Five addressing modes reach all of it: direct (the whole space), indirect with displacement (63 locations from the base in Y or Z), indirect, indirect with pre-decrement and indirect with post-increment (X, Y and Z).
An internal SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles.

512 bytes, 1 Kbyte or 2 Kbytes of EEPROM in its own data space, read and written a byte at a time, endurance at least 100,000 write/erase cycles. Its address, data and control registers are in the I/O space. A self-timing function lets software see when the next byte can be written, and a specific write sequence guards against accidental writes. A read halts the CPU for four clocks and a write for two before the next instruction.

Too low a VCC corrupts EEPROM data two ways: a write needs a minimum voltage to complete correctly, and the CPU itself can misexecute instructions. Keeping RESET asserted whenever the supply is insufficient prevents both; the internal brown-out detector does this, and an external low-VCC reset circuit serves when no BOD level fits. A reset arriving mid-write lets the write finish as long as the supply holds up.

All I/O and peripherals sit in the I/O space, reachable with LD/LDS/LDD and ST/STS/STD. Registers at 0x00 - 0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI and CBI and testable with SBIS and SBIC; IN and OUT use I/O addresses 0x00 - 0x3F, and data space addresses are 0x20 higher. Reserved bits are written as zero and reserved addresses never written. Some status flags clear by writing a one; on this device SBI and CBI act on the named bit only, so they are safe on such registers. Three general-purpose I/O registers, GPIOR0/1/2, hold any data; those in 0x00 - 0x1F are bit-accessible.

The AVR clock control unit, fed by the system clock prescaler, gives clkCPU (core, register file, status register, stack), clkI/O (most I/O modules such as the timers and SPI, and the external interrupt edge detection), clkFLASH (Flash interface, normally active with clkCPU) and clkADC (a separate domain so the CPU and I/O clocks can stop during conversions for less noise). clkPLL clocks the fast peripherals from 64 MHz or 32 MHz, and a 16 MHz clock for the CPU is derived from it. Unused domains can be stopped by the sleep modes. A level interrupt used to wake from power-down must be held until the start-up time ends, or the part wakes without taking the interrupt.

The CKSEL fuses pick the clock source and the source of the PLL input. On waking from power-down the selected source times the start-up so the oscillator is stable before code runs. From reset an extra delay, timed by the watchdog oscillator, lets the supply settle first.

The part ships with CKSEL = 0010, SUT = 10 and CKDIV8 programmed: the internal RC oscillator, the longest start-up time and the system clock divided by eight, a setting every in-system or parallel programmer can work with.

XTAL1 and XTAL2 are the input and output of an inverting amplifier for a quartz crystal or ceramic resonator. It is a low-power oscillator with reduced swing on XTAL2 and cannot drive other clock inputs. C1 and C2 are always equal; the best value depends on the crystal or resonator, stray capacitance and the noise environment. CKSEL3..1 selects one of three frequency ranges, and CKSEL0 with SUT1..0 the start-up time.

Gives 8.0 MHz nominal, voltage- and temperature-dependent, and needs no external parts. At reset hardware loads the factory calibration value into OSCCAL; software can write OSCCAL for finer calibration than the factory value. The watchdog timer and reset time-out still run from the watchdog oscillator when this oscillator clocks the chip.

The internal PLL multiplies a nominal 1 MHz input, the internal RC oscillator divided down, by 64. Because it is locked to the RC oscillator, OSCCAL changes move the fast peripheral clock too; if the divided RC oscillator is pushed above 1 MHz the PLL loses lock and the fast clock saturates at 70 MHz worst case, so OSCCAL is kept from taking the input above 1 MHz. PLLE in PLLCSR turns the PLL on and PLOCK reports lock. The 1 MHz RC output and the PLL are off in power-down and standby. The PLL output divided by 2 is clkPLL; divided by 4 it can be the system clock.
A low-power 128 kHz oscillator, nominal at 3 V and 25 °C, that clocks the watchdog.

An external clock drives XTAL1 with CKSEL = 0000, from 0 to 16 MHz. A cycle-to-cycle frequency change above 2% can make the MCU behave unpredictably; for larger steps hold it in reset. The system clock prescaler changes the internal frequency at run time safely.

With the CKOUT fuse programmed the system clock appears on CLKO (PD1), also during reset, overriding the pin's I/O function. Any clock source can be output; with the prescaler in use, the divided clock is output.

CLKPR divides the system clock (clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU, clkFLASH) for any clock source to save power. Changes are glitch-free and no intermediate frequency exceeds either the old or the new one. The new division takes effect between T1 + T2 and T1 + 2 x T2 after CLKPS[3:0] is written, T1 being the old period and T2 the new. To change it, write CLKPCE = 1 with all other bits zero (CLKPR = 0x80), then within four cycles write CLKPS with CLKPCE = 0 (CLKPR = 0x0N), with interrupts disabled.

Set SE in SMCR and execute SLEEP; SM[2:0] in SMCR picks the mode. An enabled interrupt wakes the MCU, which halts four cycles beyond the start-up time, runs the interrupt routine and continues after SLEEP. Register file and SRAM keep their contents. A reset during sleep wakes the part to the reset vector.

SM[2:0] = 000. The CPU and Flash clocks stop; SPI, UART, analog comparator, timers, watchdog and interrupts keep running. External and internal interrupts such as timer overflow wake the part. Setting ACD in ACSR powers the comparator down when it need not wake the part.

SM[2:0] = 001. clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH stop while the ADC, external interrupts, the timer (in asynchronous mode only) and the watchdog run. With the ADC enabled, a conversion starts on entry. Besides ADC conversion complete, the part wakes on external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, a timer interrupt, SPM/EEPROM ready, an external level interrupt or a pin change.

SM[2:0] = 010. The external oscillator stops; external interrupts and the watchdog keep working. Wake-up comes from an external reset, watchdog reset or interrupt, brown-out reset, an external level interrupt or a pin change. All generated clocks stop, leaving only asynchronous modules. The wake-up delay is set by the same CKSEL fuses as the reset time-out, and a wake-up level must last until the start-up time ends.
SM[2:0] = 110 with an external clock option selected. Like power-down but the oscillator keeps running; the part wakes in six clock cycles.

PRR stops the clock of individual peripherals; a stopped peripheral freezes and its I/O registers cannot be read or written. Its resources stay taken, so the peripheral is normally disabled first. Clearing the bit restores it to its earlier state. It saves power in active and idle modes; in the other sleep modes the clocks are already stopped.

Use the deepest sleep mode that still works and turn off unused functions. An enabled ADC stays on in every sleep mode, and after being turned off and on its next conversion is an extended one. Disable the comparator in idle and ADC noise reduction modes; in other modes it turns off by itself, except that a comparator using the internal reference keeps the reference on in every mode. An enabled BOD or watchdog runs in all sleep modes and is a large share of the current in the deep ones. The internal reference is on whenever the BOD, comparator or ADC needs it and must be given time to start after being turned on again.

operation.topic: Port pins and debug in sleep
operation.text: No pin should drive a resistive load in sleep. In modes where clkI/O and clkADC both stop, the digital input buffers are disabled except where needed for wake-up. A floating input, or one near VCC/2, draws excess current through an enabled input buffer; for analog inputs the digital buffer is kept disabled at all times with DIDR0 (ADC) and DIDR1 (comparator). With on-chip debug enabled by fuse, the main clock source stays on in sleep.

During reset every I/O register goes to its initial value and execution starts at the reset vector. The I/O ports take their initial state at once, with no clock needed. When every reset source has gone inactive, a delay counter set by the SUT and CKSEL fuses stretches the internal reset so the supply can settle. Unused interrupt vector locations can hold ordinary code.

Power-on reset (VCC below VPOT), external reset (RESET low longer than the minimum pulse), watchdog system reset (watchdog period expires with system reset mode on) and brown-out reset (VCC below VBOT with the detector on). MCUSR flags PORF, BORF, EXTRF and WDRF record which source acted. The reset pin has a pull-up and a spike filter.

An on-chip detector holds the part in reset while VCC is below its level. Rising through VPOT starts the delay counter, which sets how long the reset lasts after VCC rises; falling below the level reasserts reset at once. RESET may be tied to VCC or held low externally to extend the start-up.

A low level on RESET longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part, even with no clock; shorter pulses may not. When the pin rises past VRST the delay counter runs for tTOUT before the MCU starts. The RSTDISBL fuse disables it.

The BOD compares VCC with a level chosen by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis split evenly about VBOT. Once VCC drops under VBOT- the brown-out reset acts at once; when it rises above VBOT+ the delay counter starts the MCU after tTOUT. A dip must last longer than tBOD to be detected.
A watchdog time-out gives a reset pulse one CK cycle long; its falling edge starts the tTOUT delay.

An internal bandgap reference serves the brown-out detector and can feed the analog comparator or the ADC. It is on only when the BOD is enabled by the BODLEVEL fuses, when ACBG in ACSR connects it to the comparator, or when the ADC is enabled; otherwise it must be given its start-up time before the comparator or ADC output is used. Avoiding all three turns it off in power-down.

The watchdog counts a separate 128 kHz on-chip oscillator and gives an interrupt, a system reset, or an interrupt followed by a reset when it reaches the time-out, selectable from 16 ms to 8 s (2K to 1024K oscillator cycles). The WDR instruction restarts the count. The interrupt can wake the part or serve as a general timer; interrupt-then-reset mode allows saving data before the reset. An enabled watchdog runs in all sleep modes. The WDTON fuse forces system reset mode, locking WDE at 1 and WDIE at 0.

Clearing WDE or changing the time-out is a timed sequence: write WDCE and WDE to one in a single operation (WDE written one whatever it held), then within four clock cycles write WDE and the WDP bits as wanted with WDCE cleared, in one operation. Reset the watchdog before changing WDP, since a shorter period can time out at once. A watchdog left on after an unintended start resets the part again and again unless the start-up code clears WDRF and WDE, which it should do even when the watchdog is not used.

Vector addresses step by two program words (0x0000, 0x0002, ... 0x003C). The BOOTRST fuse sets where reset jumps and IVSEL in MCUCR where the interrupt vectors start. Unused vector locations can hold code, as can the vector area when reset and the vectors are in different sections.

External interrupts come from the INT0 to INT3 pins and pin-change interrupts from the PCINT pins; both trigger even when the pin is an output, which gives a way to raise a software interrupt. PCI3 fires on any enabled toggle of PCINT[31:24], PCI2 of PCINT[23:16], PCI1 of PCINT[15:8] and PCI0 of PCINT[7:0], the PCMSK3 to PCMSK0 registers choosing the pins. Pin changes are detected asynchronously and can wake the part from sleep modes other than idle as well. INT pins trigger on a rising or falling edge or a low level as set in EICRA; a level interrupt fires for as long as the pin is low. Edges need the I/O clock, but the low level is detected asynchronously and wakes the part from sleep modes other than idle. A wake-up level must be held until the start-up time ends.

All ports read-modify-write: SBI and CBI change one pin's direction, value or pull-up without touching the others. The outputs are symmetrical with high sink and source capability, strong enough to drive LED displays directly. Every pin has a selectable pull-up of supply-independent resistance and protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has three I/O locations: PORTx (data), DDRx (direction), both read/write, and PINx (input pins), read-only; writing a one to a PINx bit toggles that PORTx bit. PUD in MCUCR turns off every pull-up. Using an alternate function on some pins leaves the rest of the port free for general I/O.

DDxn = 1 makes Pxn an output, 0 an input. On an input, PORTxn = 1 turns the pull-up on and 0 turns it off. On an output, PORTxn sets the level driven. Pins go tri-state as soon as reset is active, with no clock needed.

Going from tri-state (00) to output high (11) passes through pull-up on (01) or output low (10); the pull-up state is normally harmless, and PUD can disable every pull-up if it is not. Going from input with pull-up to output low passes through tri-state (00) or output high (11).

PINxn and the latch before it form a synchronizer against metastability, so a pin change appears between 1/2 and 1 1/2 system clock periods later. Reading back a value just written to PORTx needs a NOP between the OUT and the IN; the synchronizer delay is then one clock period.

In power-down and standby the SLEEP signal clamps the Schmitt trigger inputs to ground so floating or mid-supply inputs draw no current. Pins enabled as external interrupts, and some alternate functions, override the clamp. If an asynchronous interrupt pin set for rising edge, falling edge or any change is high while its interrupt is disabled, its flag is set on waking from these modes, because the clamp release looks like an edge.

Unused pins should have a defined level to keep current down in reset, active and idle modes. The internal pull-up does this, though it is off during reset; an external pull-up or pull-down covers reset too. Tying an unused pin straight to VCC or GND risks excess current if it is ever set as an output.

Most port pins also serve peripheral functions. A module overrides the pin through override signals for the pull-up (PUOE/PUOV), data direction (DDOE/DDOV), port value (PVOE/PVOV) and digital input enable (DIEOE/DIEOV), and takes the digital input DI or the analog connection AIO. The port tables list each pin's override signals.

PB7: PSCOUT0B, ADC4, SCK (input in SPI slave mode whatever DDB7 holds; DDB7 sets the direction in master mode, and PORTB7 still controls the pull-up when it is forced to input), PCINT7. PB6: ADC7, PSCOUT1B, PCINT6. PB5: ADC6, INT2, ACMPN1, AMP2-, PCINT5. PB4: AMP0+, PCINT4. PB3: AMP0-, PCINT3. PB2: ADC5, INT1, ACMPN0, PCINT2. PB1: MOSI (input in slave mode whatever DDB1 holds, set by DDB1 in master mode, pull-up still under PORTB1 and PUD), PSCOUT2B, PCINT1. PB0: MISO (input in master mode whatever DDB0 holds, set by DDB0 in slave mode, pull-up still under PORTB0 and PUD), PSCOUT2A, PCINT0. Pins used as comparator or amplifier inputs are set as inputs with the pull-up off so the digital port does not disturb them.

PC7: D2A (DAC output), AMP2+, PCINT15. PC6: ADC10, ACMP1, PCINT14. PC5: ADC9, ACMP3, AMP1+, PCINT13. PC4: ADC8, AMP1-, ACMPN3, PCINT12. PC3: T1 (Timer/Counter1 count source), RXCAN, ICP1B (Timer/Counter1 input capture), PCINT11. PC2: T0 (Timer/Counter0 count source), TXCAN, PCINT10. PC1: PSCIN1, OC1B (Timer/Counter1 compare B and PWM output; DDC1 set to one), SS_A (slave select input, active low, in SPI slave mode), PCINT9. PC0: PSCOUT1A, INT3, PCINT8. Comparator and amplifier inputs are set as inputs with the pull-up off.

PD7: ACMP0, PCINT23. PD6: ADC3, ACMPN2, INT0, PCINT22. PD5: ADC2, ACMP2, PCINT21. PD4: ADC1, RXD/RXLIN (an input whenever the LIN/UART receiver is on, whatever DDRD4 holds; PORTD4 = 1 then turns on the pull-up), ICP1 (Timer/Counter1 input capture), SCK_A (alternate SPI clock), PCINT20. PD3: TXD/TXLIN (an output whenever the LIN/UART transmitter is on, whatever DDD3 holds), OC0A (Timer/Counter0 compare A and PWM output; DDD3 set to one), SS (slave select input in SPI slave mode, active low), MOSI_A, PCINT19. PD2: PSCIN2, OC1A (Timer/Counter1 compare A and PWM output; DDD2 set to one), MISO_A, PCINT18. PD1: PSCIN0, CLKO (the divided system clock, output whenever the CKOUT fuse is programmed regardless of PORTD1 and DDD1, and during reset), PCINT17. PD0: PSCOUT0A, PCINT16.

PE2: XTAL2 (crystal oscillator pin 2; not available as I/O while used as a clock pin), ADC0, PCINT26. PE1: XTAL1 (crystal oscillator pin 1, used for every clock source except the internal calibrated RC oscillator; not available as I/O while used as a clock pin), OC0B (Timer/Counter0 compare B and PWM output; DDE1 set to one), PCINT25. PE0: RESET (with RSTDISBL programmed it is an ordinary I/O and only power-on and brown-out resets remain; unprogrammed, it is the reset input and not an I/O, and DDE0, PORTE0 and PINE0 all read 0), OCD (on-chip debug I/O), PCINT24.

TC0 is an 8-bit timer/counter with two independent output compare units (A and B) whose compare registers are double buffered. It offers auto-reload on compare match (CTC), phase correct PWM without glitches, a variable PWM period and frequency generation. It has three interrupt sources: overflow TOV0 and compare matches OCF0A and OCF0B. It is powered through the PRTIM0 bit of the power reduction register PRR.

TCNT0, OCR0A and OCR0B are 8-bit registers. All TC0 interrupt flags sit in TIFR0 and each is masked in TIMSK0. The counter is clocked from the prescaler or from an external clock on the T0 pin; the clock select bits CS0[2:0] in TCCR0B pick the source and edge, and with no source selected the timer is stopped. The selected clock is called clkT0. OCR0A and OCR0B are compared with TCNT0 continuously; a match can drive the OC0A/OC0B pins and sets OCF0A/OCF0B.

Each clkT0 the counter is cleared, incremented or decremented according to the mode. TCNT0 can be read and written by the CPU whether or not clkT0 runs, and a CPU write takes priority over any count or clear. The count sequence is set by WGM01 and WGM00 in TCCR0A and WGM02 in TCCR0B, and TOV0 is set according to that mode.

When TCNT0 equals OCR0A or OCR0B, the compare flag OCF0A or OCF0B is set on the next timer clock; it raises an interrupt if enabled and is cleared by running the interrupt or by writing a one to it. The waveform generator uses the match with the WGM0 and COM0x[1:0] settings. In the PWM modes OCR0x is double buffered and the compare register is updated at TOP or BOTTOM, which keeps PWM pulses symmetrical and glitch free; in normal and CTC modes the buffer is off and the CPU writes OCR0x directly.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter0 force compare and TCNT0 writes
operation.text: In non-PWM modes writing a one to FOC0x in TCCR0C forces a compare match: the OC0x pin changes as COM0x[1:0] dictates, but OCF0x is not set and the timer is not cleared or reloaded. Any CPU write to TCNT0 blocks a compare match in the next timer clock, even with the timer stopped, so OCR0x can be loaded with the TCNT0 value without an interrupt. Writing TCNT0 equal to OCR0x therefore loses that match, and TCNT0 should not be written to BOTTOM while counting down. Set OC0x up before making the pin an output; the force bits in normal mode are the simplest way. OC0x keeps its value across mode changes. COM0x[1:0] is not double buffered and acts at once.

COM0x[1:0] sets what the waveform generator does to the internal OC0x register at the next match and whether the pin is driven by OC0x. Reset clears OC0x to 0. With either COM0x bit set, OC0x replaces the port value, but the pin's DDR bit must be set to output for it to appear; this holds in every waveform mode. COM0x[1:0] = 0 means no action at a match. A change of COM0x[1:0] takes effect at the next match; in non-PWM modes FOC0x applies it at once. Some COM0x settings are reserved in some modes, and COM0x has no effect on input capture.

WGM0[2:0] = 0x0. The counter counts up, rolls over from 0xFF to 0x00, and TOV0 is set in the clock cycle TCNT0 becomes zero, acting as a ninth bit that is only set. A new count can be written at any time. The compare units can time interrupts; generating waveforms in this mode costs much CPU time and is not recommended.

WGM0[2:0] = 0x2. The counter clears when TCNT0 matches OCR0A, so OCR0A sets TOP and the resolution; OCF0A can interrupt at each TOP to update it. CTC mode has no double buffering of OCR0A: writing a value below the current TCNT0 misses the match and the counter runs to 0xFF and wraps before matching. With COM0A[1:0] = 0x1 OC0A toggles at each match (visible only with the pin set as output), at most fclk_I/O/2 with OCR0A = 0x00. TOV0 is set when the counter wraps from MAX to 0x00.

WGM0[2:0] = 0x3 (TOP = 0xFF) or 0x7 (TOP = OCR0A). Single slope: the counter counts BOTTOM to TOP, then clears on the next timer clock, giving up to twice the frequency of the phase correct modes. TOV0 is set at TOP. COM0x[1:0] = 0x2 gives non-inverted PWM (OC0x cleared at match, set at BOTTOM), 0x3 inverted. With WGM02 set, COM0A[1:0] = 0x1 toggles OC0A at each match, a 50% square wave of at most fclk_I/O/2 with OCR0A = 0x00 (double buffered, unlike CTC); OC0B has no toggle option. OCR0A = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 timer clocks; OCR0A = MAX holds the output at one level, high or low by the COM0A[1:0] polarity.

WGM0[2:0] = 0x1 (TOP = 0xFF) or 0x5 (TOP = OCR0A). Dual slope: the counter counts BOTTOM to TOP and back, staying at TOP for one timer clock; it is slower than fast PWM but symmetrical, which suits motor control. Non-inverting (COM0x[1:0] = 0x2): OC0x clears at the match while counting up and sets at the match while counting down; 0x3 inverts. With WGM02 set, COM0A0 = 1 toggles OC0A at matches; OC0B has no toggle option. TOV0 is set at BOTTOM. OCR0A = BOTTOM gives a constant low, MAX a constant high (non-inverted). OC0x can change at BOTTOM without a match, to keep the waveform symmetrical: when OCR0x changes from MAX, and when the timer starts counting up from above OCR0x and so misses the up-count match.

The timer is synchronous: clkT0 acts as a clock enable on clkI/O. TOV0 sets as TCNT0 goes from MAX to BOTTOM; OCF0x sets on the timer clock after TCNT0 equals OCR0x (OCF0B in every mode, OCF0A except where OCR0A is TOP); in CTC and in fast PWM with OCR0A as TOP, OCF0A sets and TCNT0 clears to BOTTOM on the clock after TOP. The same holds with the prescaler, one timer clock per N I/O clocks.

TC1 is a 16-bit timer/counter (true 16-bit PWM) with two independent output compare units with double buffered compare registers, one input capture unit with a noise canceler, clear-timer-on-compare-match, glitch-free phase correct PWM, variable PWM period, a frequency generator and an external event counter. Its interrupt sources are TOV1, OCF1A, OCF1B and ICF1. The input capture trigger can come from the ICP1 pin or the analog comparator output.

TCNT1, OCR1A, OCR1B and ICR1 are 16-bit registers, read and written in two byte accesses; TCCR1A/B/C are 8-bit with no access limits. Flags are in TIFR1, masks in TIMSK1. The clock comes from the prescaler or the T1 pin, selected by CS1[2:0] in TCCR1B (no source: stopped); it is called clkT1. TOP can be OCR1A, ICR1 or a fixed value. With OCR1A as TOP in a PWM mode, OCR1A cannot drive a PWM output but TOP is double buffered and can be changed while running; with ICR1 as TOP (fixed), OCR1A stays free for PWM.

One 8-bit TEMP register holds the high byte for every 16-bit access in TC1. Writing the low byte copies TEMP and the low byte into the 16-bit register in one clock; reading the low byte copies the high byte into TEMP. So write high byte then low byte, and read low byte then high byte. Reading OCR1A/B does not use TEMP. If an interrupt between the two accesses also uses TEMP, the result is corrupted: when both main code and interrupts touch 16-bit timer registers, the main code disables interrupts for the access. When several registers share the same high byte, it need only be written once (the same atomic rule applies). A C compiler handles the byte order itself.

TCNT1 is mapped as TCNT1H and TCNT1L; TCNT1H is reached through TEMP, so the whole 16-bit count is read or written in one clock cycle. Writing TCNT1 while it counts gives unpredictable results in some cases (named under each mode). The counter is cleared, incremented or decremented each clkT1 by the mode; the CPU can access TCNT1 with or without clkT1 and a CPU write wins over count and clear. The sequence is set by WGM1[3:2] in TCCR1B and WGM1[1:0] in TCCR1A; TOV1 is set according to the mode.

A logic change on ICP1, or on the analog comparator output ACO, that matches the edge setting copies TCNT1 into ICR1 and sets ICF1 in the same system clock; ICF1 interrupts if TIMSK1.ICIE is set and clears when the interrupt runs or when a one is written to it. Read ICR1 low byte first. ICR1 can be written only in modes that use it as TOP, after WGM1[3:0] has been set, high byte first. The comparator is chosen as trigger with ACIC in ACSR; changing the trigger source can cause a capture, so clear ICF1 afterwards. ICP1 and ACO are sampled like the T1 pin. The capture input is active except in modes that use ICR1 as TOP. Driving the ICP1 port pin from software can trigger a capture.

Enabled with ICNC in TCCR1B, the noise canceler requires four equal samples of the input before the edge detector sees a change, adding four system clock cycles of delay before ICR1 updates. It runs on the system clock and is not affected by the prescaler.

ICR1 is overwritten by the next event if it has not been read, so read it as early as possible in the interrupt; the worst-case latency depends on the longest other interrupt handler. Changing TOP while capturing is not recommended. To measure duty cycle, change the edge setting right after reading ICR1, then clear ICF1 by writing a one; for frequency alone (with an interrupt handler) ICF1 need not be cleared. In normal mode the interval between events must not exceed the counter range, or the overflow interrupt or the prescaler must extend it.

When TCNT1 equals OCR1x, OCF1x is set on the next timer clock and interrupts if OCIE1x is set; it clears when the interrupt runs or by writing a one. Unit A can also set TOP, which sets the waveform period. OCR1x is double buffered in all twelve PWM modes and updated at TOP or BOTTOM; in normal and CTC modes the CPU writes it directly. OCR1x is written through TEMP, high byte first; the low-byte write moves both bytes into the buffer or compare register in one clock.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter1 force compare and TCNT1 writes
operation.text: In non-PWM modes writing a one to FOC1x in TCCR1C forces a match on OC1x without setting OCF1x or clearing the timer. A CPU write to TCNT1 blocks any match in the next timer clock, even when stopped. Writing TCNT1 equal to OCR1x loses that match; writing TCNT1 equal to TOP in a PWM mode with variable TOP loses the TOP match and the counter runs on to 0xFFFF; do not write BOTTOM while counting down. Set OC1x before making its pin an output. OC1x keeps its value across mode changes. COM1x[1:0] is not double buffered and acts at once.

COM1x[1:0] in TCCR1A sets the internal OC1x state at the next match and whether OC1x drives the pin; reset clears OC1x to 0. With either COM1x bit set, OC1x replaces the port value but appears only with the pin's DDR bit set to output; this override is mostly independent of mode, with some exceptions. COM1x[1:0] = 0 means no action at a match; a change acts at the next match, or at once through FOC1x in non-PWM modes. Some settings are reserved in some modes; COM1x has no effect on input capture.

WGM1[3:0] = 0x0. The counter counts up and rolls over from MAX = 0xFFFF to 0x0000; TOV1 is set in the timer clock TCNT1 becomes zero, like a 17th bit that is only set. A new count can be written any time. Compare units can time interrupts; generating waveforms in normal mode is not recommended.

Mode 4 (WGM1[3:0] = 0x4, TOP = OCR1A) or mode 12 (0xC, TOP = ICR1). TCNT1 clears when it matches TOP; OCF1A or ICF1 can interrupt at each TOP. TOP is not double buffered: a new value below TCNT1 misses the match and the counter runs to 0xFFFF and wraps. Fast PWM with OCR1A as TOP (WGM1[3:0] = 0xF) is the double-buffered alternative. With COM1A[1:0] = 0x1 OC1A toggles at each match (pin set as output, DDR_OC1A = 1), at most fclk_I/O/2 with OCR1A = 0x0000. TOV1 is set when the counter goes from MAX to 0x0000.

Modes 5, 6, 7, 14 and 15 (WGM1[3:0] = 0x5, 0x6, 0x7, 0xE, 0xF): single slope, BOTTOM to TOP then clear on the next timer clock. TOP is 0x00FF, 0x01FF or 0x03FF (8, 9 or 10 bits), ICR1 (0xE) or OCR1A (0xF); the resolution runs from 2 bits (TOP = 0x0003) to 16 bits (TOP = MAX). TOV1 is set at TOP, and with OCR1A or ICR1 as TOP, OCF1A or ICF1 is set in the same clock. A new TOP must not be below any compare register, or no match happens; with fixed TOP the unused OCR1x bits are masked to zero on write. ICR1 is not double buffered: set lower than TCNT1 it misses TOP and the counter runs to 0xFFFF; OCR1A is double buffered and loaded at TOP, together with the clear and TOV1. ICR1 suits a fixed TOP (freeing OCR1A for PWM); OCR1A suits a TOP that changes. OCR1x = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every TOP+1 timer clocks; OCR1x = TOP a constant level. With OCR1A as TOP and COM1A[1:0] = 0x1, OC1A toggles at 50% duty, at most fclk_I/O/2 with OCR1A = 0x0000.

In fast PWM, COM1x[1:0] = 0x2 gives a non-inverted PWM output and 0x3 an inverted one; OC1x is set (or cleared) at the match and cleared (or set) when the counter goes from TOP to BOTTOM. The output appears only with DDR_OC1x set. Misprint: the fast PWM paragraph calls 0x2 inverted and 0x3 non-inverted; it should read the other way round.

WGM1[3:0] = 0x1, 0x2, 0x3 (TOP 0x00FF, 0x01FF, 0x03FF), 0xA (TOP = ICR1) or 0xB (TOP = OCR1A); resolution 2 to 16 bits. Dual slope from BOTTOM (0x0000) to TOP and back, TCNT1 = TOP for one clock; slower than fast PWM but symmetrical, preferred for motor control. Non-inverting (COM1x[1:0] = 0x2): OC1x clears at the match counting up and sets at the match counting down; 0x3 inverts. TOV1 is set at BOTTOM; OCF1A or ICF1 is set at TOP when OCR1x is loaded from its buffer. A new TOP must not be below the compare registers, and fixed TOP masks unused OCR1x bits. Because OCR1x updates at TOP, changing TOP while running makes the falling and rising slopes differ and the output asymmetric; the phase and frequency correct mode is recommended for a changing TOP, and with a fixed TOP the two behave practically the same. OCR1x = BOTTOM gives constant low, TOP constant high (non-inverted); with WGM1[3:0] = 0xB and COM1A[1:0] = 0x1 OC1A toggles at 50% duty.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter1 phase and frequency correct PWM mode
operation.text: WGM1[3:0] = 0x8 (TOP = ICR1) or 0x9 (TOP = OCR1A); resolution 2 bits (TOP = 0x0003) to 16 bits. Dual slope like phase correct PWM, but OCR1x is loaded from its buffer at BOTTOM, so both slopes of every period are equal and the output is symmetrical in all periods. TOV1 is set at BOTTOM, with the OCR1x update; OCF1A or ICF1 is set at TOP. A new TOP must not be below the compare registers. ICR1 suits a fixed TOP, OCR1A a changing one. COM1x[1:0] = 0x2 gives non-inverted PWM, 0x3 inverted; pin needs DDR_OC1x set. OCR1x = BOTTOM gives constant low, TOP high (non-inverted); with WGM1[3:0] = 0x9 and COM1A[1:0] = 0x1 OC1A toggles at 50% duty.

clkT1 acts as a clock enable on clkI/O. OCF1x sets on the timer clock after TCNT1 equals OCR1x. In CTC and fast PWM the count goes TOP to BOTTOM; in the two dual-slope PWM modes it goes TOP to TOP-1. TOV1 (fast PWM) and ICF1 (when ICR1 is TOP) set as the count leaves TOP, where OCR1x takes its new value. In phase and frequency correct mode the update happens at BOTTOM instead, and the same holds for modes that set TOV1 at BOTTOM. With the prescaler the steps are one timer clock per N I/O clocks.

TC0 and TC1 share one free-running 10-bit prescaler but choose their settings separately. CSn[2:0] = 0x1 clocks the timer straight from the system clock (fCLK_I/O, the fastest); the taps give fCLK_I/O/8, /64, /256 and /1024. Because the prescaler runs regardless of the timer's clock select, the first count after enabling a prescaled timer comes 1 to N+1 system clocks later (N = 8, 64, 256 or 1024). Resetting the prescaler with PSR10 synchronises a timer to program execution but changes the prescaler period for the other timer too.

A clock on T0 or T1 is sampled every system clock by synchroniser latches and passed to an edge detector, which gives one timer clock per rising edge (CSn[2:0] = 0x7) or falling edge (0x6). The path delays the count by 2.5 to 3.5 system clocks. Switch the input on or off only once the pin has held its level for a system clock or more; otherwise a spurious count can occur. Each half period must exceed one system clock: fTn < fclk_I/O/2 at 50% duty, and below fclk_I/O/2.5 is recommended to allow for oscillator tolerance. An external clock cannot be prescaled.

The PSC is a waveform controller for external power stages: six programmable complementary outputs (three half-bridges, for three-phase asynchronous or BLDC motor drives, lighting, DC/DC converters), programmable dead time, PWM up to 12-bit resolution, a PWM clock up to 64 MHz from the PLL, a programmable ADC trigger, automatic overlap protection, three fail-safe emergency inputs that force the outputs to high impedance or to their inactive state (fuse configurable), and centre-aligned or edge-aligned operation. Each output can be set active high or active low.

16-bit PSC registers are accessed as two bytes through one temporary register shared by all PSC 16-bit registers: write the high byte then the low byte, read the low byte then the high byte. The low-byte access makes the 16-bit transfer in one clock.

A free-running 12-bit PSC counter counts up to the value in POCR_RB, then counts down or resets to zero, depending on the running mode. The PSC has three modules (0, 1, 2). Each module has a part A that drives PSCOUTnA and a part B that drives PSCOUTnB, overlap protection, and its own input circuit for PSCINn (or the matching analog comparator output AC0O, AC1O, AC2O). The clock is CLKIO or CLKPLL through a prescaler.

Each PSC cycle is sub-cycle A (PSCOUTnA) followed by sub-cycle B (PSCOUTnB). New register settings take effect at the end of the cycle, after sub-cycle B, whichever ramp mode is used. The mode, One Ramp or Center Aligned, applies to all waveform generators. In Center Aligned mode the counter counts up then down.

The waveform is set by POCRnSA, POCRnRA, POCRnSB, POCR_RB and the running mode. One Ramp mode: all three B outputs share their edges, and the A outputs do as well when loaded with equal values; the PWM frequency is twice that of Center Aligned mode. Center Aligned mode: all six outputs are centred in the period, so unless the duty cycles match their edges do not coincide and switching noise is lower; the PWM frequency is half that of One Ramp mode. With overlap protection off, PSCOUTnA and PSCOUTnB can be made to overlap in One Ramp mode. With PCCYC = 1 in PCTL, starting and stopping the PSC waits for the end of a complete cycle.

operation.topic: PSC Center Aligned mode and POCRnRA
operation.text: In Center Aligned mode POCRnRA plays no part in the output timing, so it is free to set the ADC synchronisation point.

All timing values are updated together at the end of a PSC cycle so no cycle mixes old and new values; software computes the new set and requests the update. Software can also stop the cycle early, update and restart. While the LOCK bit is set, new values written during a cycle are held; clearing LOCK lets the whole set load at the end of the cycle. LOCK covers POC, POCR0SA, POCR1SA, POCR2SA, POCR0RA, POCR1RA, POCR2RA, POCR0SB, POCR1SB, POCR2SB and POCR_RB.
Overlap protection keeps the two outputs of one module from being active at the same time, preventing cross conduction. It can be turned off with POVEn.

Each module takes one PSC input, set up by its PSC module n input control register PMICn, which also configures parts A and B. PSCINn acts as a retrigger or a fault input. The input source is the PSCINn pin or analog comparator n output (PISELnx), optionally through a digital filter, with edge or level sensing and the input mode PRFMnx[3:0].

operation.topic: PSC input filter and asynchronous output control
operation.text: With the filter enable bit set, a digital filter of four PSC clock cycles precedes the input; turning it off is mainly for prescaled PSC clocks, where the filter's delay is too long. A fault input normally acts on the outputs through the PSC, which needs CLKPSC running; with the asynchronous output control bit PAOCnA/B set, PSCINn deactivates the PSC outputs directly, and the input is still processed normally once CLKPSC runs. With the filter active, level sensing still deactivates the outputs even when the PSC clock is disturbed.

PELEVnx selects the active edge (edge modes) or level (level modes): set, the rising edge or the high level; clear, the falling edge or the low level. In 2- or 4-ramp mode, input A counts only during Dead-Time0 and On-Time0, and input B during Dead-Time1 and On-Time1. In 1-ramp mode either input acts over the whole ramp.
In these modes the active input deactivates the selected outputs without changing the PSC timing. The input acts alike on On-Time0/Dead-Time0 and On-Time1/Dead-Time1.
The active input halts the PSC, which waits for software action: setting PRUNn in PCTLn. In fault mode 7 either input acts alike on On-Time0/Dead-Time0 or On-Time1/Dead-Time1.

Each PSC module produces a signal that synchronises the ADC sample and hold, and measurements need it. It can be taken from any rising or falling edge of PSCOUTnA or PSCOUTnB. In Center Aligned mode POCRnRA is unused and can set the synchronisation point; its minimum value is then 1.

Each PSC has its own interrupt sources: counter reload (end of On-Time 1), a PSC input event (active edge, or start of an active level) and a PSC mutual synchronisation error. There are two vectors: PSC_End, on a match with POCR_RB when enabled, and PSC_Fault, when an input detects a fault event and it is enabled.
A PSC is clocked from either the PLL (CLK PLL) or the I/O clock (CLK I/O). PCLKSELn in PCTL chooses the source and PPREn1/0 in PCTL the division factor.

The SPI is a full-duplex three-wire synchronous serial interface: master or slave, LSB or MSB first, seven programmable bit rates, an end-of-transmission interrupt flag, write collision protection, wake-up from idle mode and a double-speed (CK/2) master mode. It is enabled by writing PRSPI in PRR to 0. The master clock divider offers /2, /4, /8, /16, /32, /64 and /128, with SPI2X selecting double speed.

A master starts a transfer by pulling the chosen slave's SS low; both sides load their shift registers and the master clocks SCK, shifting data out on MOSI and in on MISO, then raises SS to end the packet. As master the SPI does not drive SS itself; software must. Writing SPDR starts the clock; after eight bits the clock stops and SPIF is set, raising an interrupt if SPIE in SPCR is set. As slave, while SS is high the SPI sleeps with MISO tri-stated and SPDR can be loaded; data shifts only while SS is low, and SPIF sets after each byte. The last received byte stays in the buffer register.

Transmit is single buffered: SPDR cannot be written until the whole shift is done. Receive is double buffered: a received byte must be read before the next is completely shifted in, or the first is lost. In slave mode SCK is sampled, so its low and high periods must each be longer than two CPU clock cycles.

As slave, SS is always an input. Held low it activates the SPI and MISO becomes an output if so configured, all other pins inputs. Driven high, all pins are inputs, the SPI ignores incoming data and its logic resets, dropping any partly received byte; this keeps the slave's bit counter in step with the master.

As master (MSTR set) the SS direction is the user's. As an output it is a general output that does not affect the SPI, typically driving a slave's SS. As an input it has to stay high for master operation; if pulled low, the SPI takes it as another master selecting it: MSTR is cleared so the SPI becomes a slave and MOSI and SCK become inputs, and SPIF is set, interrupting if enabled with the I-bit set. Interrupt-driven masters should check that MSTR is still set and set it again if a slave select cleared it.
CPOL and CPHA in SPCR give four combinations of clock polarity and phase; data is shifted out and latched on opposite SCK edges so it has time to settle. DORD = 0 sends MSB first, DORD = 1 LSB first.

A full CAN controller meeting CAN 2.0A and 2.0B (it is a 2.0B active node: it handles both 11-bit and 29-bit identifiers). It has six message objects (MObs), each with its own identifier tag and mask (11 bits for 2.0A, 29 bits for 2.0B), an 8-byte data buffer, a choice of transmit, receive, frame-buffer or automatic reply use, and a time stamp. It reaches 1 Mbit/s with an 8 MHz clock, has a TTC timer and a listening mode for bus monitoring or automatic baud detection. It handles data, remote, error and overload frames and covers the LLC and MAC sublayers and the PLS sublayer of the physical layer; the PMA and MDI sublayers are not supported.

CAN is a broadcast, message-oriented bus defined in ISO 11898 (high speed) and ISO 11519-2 (low speed). Each message identifier is unique on the network and sets the message priority: the lower the binary value, the higher the priority. Contention is settled bit by bit on the identifier in a wired-AND fashion, a dominant level overriding a recessive one; a node that sends recessive and sees dominant drops out and becomes a receiver, and retries only once the bus is free. A data frame beats a remote frame with the same identifier (RTR bit), and a standard frame beats an extended frame with the same base identifier.

A standard (2.0A) frame carries an 11-bit identifier, an extended (2.0B) frame an 11-bit base identifier plus an 18-bit extension; the IDE bit is dominant for standard and recessive for extended frames. A frame runs: start of frame, arbitration field (identifier and RTR, which marks a remote frame), control field (IDE and a 4-bit data length code), 0 to 8 data bytes, a 15-bit CRC with delimiter, the ACK slot and delimiter, 7 bits of end of frame and a 3-bit intermission. Receivers that received the frame correctly overwrite the recessive ACK slot with a dominant bit, whatever their acceptance filtering. In a remote frame the DLC gives the number of data bytes requested. Modules are of three kinds: 2.0A treats a 29-bit identifier as an error, 2.0B passive ignores it, and 2.0B active handles both lengths.

operation.topic: CAN bit timing in the protocol
operation.text: A node resynchronises on the falling edge of SOF and on every recessive-to-dominant edge. A bit is four segments, each a whole number of time quanta (TQ): the synchronisation segment, where an edge is expected; the propagation segment, which absorbs bus and transceiver delays; phase segment 1, which may be lengthened; and phase segment 2, which may be shortened. The bus is sampled at the end of phase segment 1. The information processing time is fixed at 2 TQ, so phase segment 2 is at least 2 TQ and no longer than phase segment 1. The resynchronisation jump width limits how far the phase segments move and is no longer than phase segment 2. An early sample point leaves more TQ in phase segment 2, so the jump width can be at its largest and cheaper oscillators such as ceramic resonators can be tolerated; a late sample point leaves more TQ for propagation and so longer buses. Hard synchronisation restarts the bit on the SOF edge; resynchronisation happens when an edge falls outside the synchronisation segment.

Errors are flagged as soon as they are found. At message level: CRC check, frame (format) check of the fixed fields and frame size, and ACK check by the sender. At bit level: monitoring, where a sender compares each bit it sends with the bus, and bit stuffing on the NRZ coding, which also provides the synchronisation edges. A node that finds an error sends an error flag to abort the transmission, and the sender retries the aborted message on its own.

Each message to send or receive has a message object holding its identifier, data and status. The application sets the MObs up at initialisation; a received frame is stored only if its identifier matches a receive MOb, and the application is then interrupted. A remote frame can be answered by the controller with the matching data frame without CPU work. The data buffers together are 120 bytes. MOb 0 has the highest priority.

Enabled: the internal TxCAN and RxCAN paths and the input clock run. Standby: the transmitter holds a recessive level, the receiver is off, the clock still runs and the registers and MOb pages stay accessible. Listening: internal TxCAN is looped back to internal RxCAN, the TXCAN pin (PD5) stays recessive, the RXCAN pin (PD6) stays enabled, and the TEC and REC error counters are frozen.

The bit-timing state machines run from the time quantum, made from clkIO by the baud rate prescaler BRP. SYNS is 1 TQ; PRS is 1 to 8 TQ; PHS1 is 1 to 8 TQ; PHS2 is no more than PHS1 and no less than the 2 TQ information processing time; SJW is 1 to min(4, PHS1). A bit holds 8 to 25 TQ in all. With no prescaling (BRP = 0) the sample point comes one TQ early, which fails the ISO 16845 test plan; PHS1 is then lengthened and PHS2 shortened by one TQ to compensate.
Setting OVRQ requests an overload frame, which the channel sends after the next reception; OVRF (OVFG) is set while it is being sent.

A MOb is a descriptor of one CAN frame, and the MObs form the front of the mailbox. They work independently; when several match, the lowest-numbered wins. Modes: disabled, transmit, receive, automatic reply and frame buffer receive. This device has six MObs, numbered 0 to 5. After reset no MOb has a defined mode, so each one is configured (for example disabled, CONMOB = 00) before the CAN peripheral is enabled.

Transmit: load the identifier tag (IDT), IDE, RTRTAG, DLC, reserved-bit tags (RBnTAG) and data, then set CONMOB. The channel picks the highest-priority MOb in transmit and sends it; TXOK is set (with an interrupt) when it is done, and the MOb keeps its contents until reinitialised. Receive: load IDT, the identifier mask IDMSK, IDE and IDEMSK, RTRTAG and RTRMSK, DLC and RBnTAG, then set CONMOB. On an incoming identifier the channel picks the highest-priority matching MOb, copies the received IDT, IDE and DLC into it, stores the data bytes (not for a remote frame) and sets RXOK with an interrupt. Automatic reply: set RPLV as well; when the remote frame matches, RTRTAG and RPLV are cleared without a flag and the MOb sends its data frame using the received identifier, tags and DLC, setting TXOK when done.

For receiving several frames: the MObs put in this mode (not necessarily consecutive) form one set, and only one set can exist. They are set up like receive MObs and each sets RXOK as it fills; BXOK is set (with an interrupt) when the last MOb of the set has received. BXOK can be cleared only after every CONMOB field of the set has been rewritten.

A frame hits a MOb when the received ID, RTR, RBn and IDE equal the MOb's IDT, RTRTAG, RBnTAG and IDE in every bit the mask enables; the received values are then written into the MOb. Examples for 2.0A: to accept only ID 0x317, mask 111 1111 1111b with tag 011 0001 0111b; to accept 0x310 to 0x317, mask 111 1111 1000b with tag 011 0001 0xxxb; to accept every ID from 0x000 to 0x7FF, mask 000 0000 0000b.

operation.topic: CAN MOb pages and data buffers
operation.text: Each MOb sits in a page whose number, written to CANPAGE, is the MOb number; other page numbers are reserved for factory test. CANHPMOB gives the highest-priority MOb flagged in CANSIT, in a form that can be written straight to CANPAGE, and is updated only for the sources enabled by ENRX, ENTX and ENERR. Each MOb's 8-byte data buffer is read and written as a FIFO via CANMSG, with INDX selecting the byte; the index increments after each access unless AINC is set, and wraps from 7 to 0. The first byte of a frame is at index 0.

A 16-bit timer stamps messages and supports time-triggered communication. Its clock is clkIO / 8 divided again by the 8-bit prescaler CANTCON, and runs while the CAN controller is enabled. It counts up from 0x0000 once ENFG is set and interrupts (OVRTIM) on rolling over from 0xFFFF. TTC mode synchronises on start of frame (SYNCTTC = 0) or end of frame (SYNCTTC = 1), and sends a frame only once even after an error. Each MOb that sends or receives a frame captures the timer on TXOK or RXOK.

The channel is error active (the default; it sends active error frames), error passive (it sends passive error frames and waits after a transmission before sending again) or bus off (no influence on the bus). A transmit error counter TEC and receive error counter REC drive the state; BOFF and ERRP report it. Error active becomes error passive when TEC or REC exceeds 127 and returns when both are below 127; TEC above 255 gives bus off and the BOFFIT interrupt; bus off returns to error active after 128 occurrences of 11 consecutive recessive bits. More than one counter change can happen during one message.

BERR, bit error: the bit seen differs from the bit sent (except a recessive bit seen dominant in the arbitration field or ACK slot, and a dominant bit seen while sending an error frame). SERR, stuff error: more than five consecutive bits of one level. CERR, CRC error (receive only): the CRC computed over the destuffed frame from SOF to the data field does not match. FERR, form error: a violation of the CRC delimiter, ACK delimiter, end of frame, error delimiter or overload delimiter. AERR, acknowledgement error (transmit only): no dominant bit in the ACK slot. Errors in transmission, and in reception once the identifier has matched, are recorded in the MOb; in reception before a match they are recorded at general level. After an error the channel sends an error frame, and it answers an error frame on the bus with its own.

Sources: receive complete, transmit complete, MOb errors (bit, stuff, CRC, form, acknowledge), frame buffer full, bus off, and CAN timer overrun. ENIT enables CAN interrupts in general and ENOVRT the timer overrun. A flag is set in the MOb's CANSTMOB or in the general CANGIT; with ENRX, ENTX or ENERR set, the MOb's bit in CANSIT is set too. MOb flags are cleared by software with a read-modify-write of CANSTMOB; CANGIT flags are cleared by writing 1 to them. OVRTIM also clears on entering its own handler. A form error found while transmitting also raises a bit error, so one error can give two interrupts. An error recorded in a MOb's CANSTMOB sets no general error in CANGIT.
CAN timing at high baud rates needs an accurate clock; an external crystal is the recommended source for CAN.

A LIN 2.1 controller in hardware, compatible with LIN 1.3, that can instead run as a UART. LIN: master and slave routines following the LIN 2.1 work-flow concept, automatic header handling with filtering of irrelevant frames, automatic response handling, extended error detection, hardware frame time-out, break-in-data support, automatic resynchronisation and extended frames. UART: full duplex, asynchronous, a high-resolution baud rate generator, 8 data bits with odd, even or no parity and one stop bit, overrun and framing error detection. LIN is a single-master, multi-slave, single-wire bus up to 20 kbit/s with self-synchronising slaves; the line driver and receiver follow ISO 9141.

A cluster has one master task and several slave tasks; the master node also holds a slave task. The master task decides which frame goes when, following a schedule table that gives each header's identifier and the spacing between frame starts. A frame is a header from the master (BREAK, SYNC, protected identifier) and a response from one slave (data bytes and checksum), each byte sent LSB first. The identifier sets the frame's purpose. Frames carry signals (always at the same place in the data field for a given identifier) or diagnostic messages, which use two reserved identifiers.

LIN 2.1 is a superset of LIN 1.3. A LIN 2.1 master can run a cluster of LIN 1.3 and LIN 2.1 slaves, avoiding the newer features (enhanced checksum, reconfiguration and diagnostics, automatic baud detection, response error status) with 1.3 slaves. A LIN 2.1 slave cannot work with a LIN 1.3 master. The LIN 2.1 physical layer works in a LIN 1.3 cluster but not the other way round.

The controller has Tx header, Rx header and response functions built on Rx and Tx services that are UART services, so it can switch to UART operation. Master and slave tasks meet only at the interrupt raised when a new identifier is available, from the Tx header function in a master node or the Rx header function in a slave node. Hardware flags mark the identifiers 60 (0x3C) to 63 (0x3F). Four interrupts cover LIN: LIDOK (new identifier), LRXOK (response received), LTXOK (response sent) and LERR (errors). Wake-up can use the UART wake-up with a node sending at least five low bits (0xF0) for LIN 2.1 or eight (0x80) for LIN 1.3, or a pin change interrupt on the LIN line. Extended frame identifiers 62 (0x3E) and 63 (0x3F) are reserved for user-defined and future formats.

As a UART the controller is full duplex with a local loop-back for test. Transmit has a one-character buffer, receive a two-character one (a serial register then a buffer register), with automatic flag handling. Transmit and receive are independent, so an unused direction frees its pin. The baud rate generator keeps the error within 2% at any clock frequency and target baud rate.
LENA in LINCR enables the controller; writing it to 0 disables it at once, with no wait states.

LCMD[2] = 0 selects LIN commands, LCMD[1..0] the function. Rx header / LIN abort is the resting state: the start point before a Tx header in a master, and in a slave the background header detection, which finds BREAK, resynchronises on SYNCH, receives and parity-checks the protected identifier (and in LIN 1.3 loads LINDLR with the decoded length), starts the frame time-out and checks the frame. Clearing LCMD[1..0] aborts a running function at once and sets LABORT in LINERR. Tx header, used only by the master task, sends BREAK (13 dominant bits), SYNCH (0x55) and the protected identifier from LINIDR with its check bits, at the baud rate set by LINBRR and LINBTR, then returns to Rx header / LIN abort with the flags set. Rx and Tx response follow a header sent or received; an Rx response command can be given up to the last data bit of the first byte. In LIN 1.3 the header sets LINDLR; in LIN 2.1 software sets LRXDL or LTXDL. LIN13 picks the checksum: enhanced (data and protected identifier) for LIN 2.1, classic (data only) for LIN 1.3; identifiers 60 to 63 always use classic. On an error the response stops, the flags are set and the bus is left recessive. A new BREAK and SYNCH can be detected during a response, and the new identifier is recorded. Response data pass through a FIFO reached by LINSEL and LINDAT; LRXDL and LTXDL are not tied to data access.

LCMD[2] = 1 selects UART commands: byte transfer (UART selected, Rx and Tx off), Rx byte, Tx byte, or full duplex. The LIN FIFO is off: LINDAT is the data register, LINSEL and LINDLR are unused. Receive: LRXOK flags an incoming character; reading LINDAT clears it and frees the second buffer stage, or the flag can be cleared without reading. When both stages are full a new character overwrites the second and is read with OVRERR; a framing error sets FERR. Transmit: writing LINDAT sends a character and clears LTXOK, which sets again when the character has gone. There is no transmit buffering and no transmit error detection.

The core reset resets the controller; LSWRES in LINCR is a self-clearing software reset that resets only part of it. The I/O clock clkI/O is its only clock. LIN13 = 0 (default) selects LIN 2.1, LIN13 = 1 LIN 1.3; it sets the checksum rule and has no effect on UART commands.

operation.topic: LIN/UART listening mode and busy signal
operation.text: The LIN configuration does not depend on the protocol selected. Listening mode joins internal Tx to internal Rx, disables the TXLIN pin and keeps RXLIN enabled, in LIN and in UART mode. LBUSY in LINSIR mirrors the hardware busy signal. While busy in LIN mode, LINCR (except LCMD[2..0], LENA and LSWRES), LINBRRL/H, LINDLR, LINIDR and LINDAT cannot be written, and the only commands taken are abort (LCMD[1..0] = 00, acted on at the end of the byte), kill (LENA = 0 or LCMD[2] = 0, at once) and reset (LSWRES = 1, at once); any other command is refused, sets LOVRERR and leaves the transfer running. In UART mode busy is set during a byte transmission (not reception) and locks LINCR (except LCMD[2..0], LENA, LSWRES) and LINDAT.

The baud rate comes from clki/o, the 12-bit divider LDIV[11..0] in LINBRRH:LINBRRL (0 to 4095) and LBT[5..0] in LINBTR, the number of samples per bit (0 to 63, default 32). Reception takes a majority vote of three samples.

While waiting for a header LBT is 32. On a BREAK of 11 to 28 bits (13 nominal; others are refused) the controller adjusts LBT to the received SYNCH field (0x55) and samples the protected identifier with the new value, which holds to the end of the response before returning to 32. It tolerates a clock deviation of ±20% and sets the baud rate within ±2%. LINBTR can then be read to recalibrate the oscillator. No resynchronisation is done in a master. LDISR in LINBTR allows LBT to be written by hand (mainly for UART use; LBT is at least 8 for the sampling) and disables slave resynchronisation for test. Writing LINBTR with LENA = 1 forces LBT to 0x20 and LDISR to 0; with LENA = 0 and LDISR written 1, LBT takes the written value and resynchronisation is off; with LDISR written 0, LBT is forced to 0x20 and resynchronisation is on.

During a Tx response LRXDL counts the bytes sent; during an Rx response LTXDL counts the bytes received, so after an error the count of good bytes is known. LIN 2.1: LTXDL = 0 sends only the checksum, LRXDL = 0 takes the first byte as the checksum, and a value above 8 is forced to 8 before the first byte. LIN 1.3: both fields are loaded from the length code in the protected identifier before LIDOK, so 0 and more than 8 cannot occur. Rx response: software sets LRXDL before the command; hardware clears LTXDL, which counts bytes; LRXOK follows the checksum, leaving LTXDL = LRXDL. Tx response: software sets LTXDL; hardware clears LRXDL, which counts bytes; LTXOK follows the checksum. On an error the transfer stops and the counter holds the number of bytes handled without error; error information for a byte is known only at the end of that byte. UART mode and reset force LRXDL and LTXDL to 0, and UART mode blocks writes to LINDLR.

LIDOK is set at the end of a header (Tx or Rx header function); in LIN 1.3 the length fields are updated first; it is not used in UART mode. LRXOK is set at the end of a received response, or per received character in UART mode. LTXOK is set at the end of a sent response, or per sent character in UART mode. Each can interrupt if enabled in LINENIR. LERR in LINSIR is the OR of the eight LINERR flags: LBERR (bit seen differs from bit sent; transmission aborted), LCERR (checksum test failed: the data bytes, together with the protected ID when running LIN 2.1, summed modulo 256 and inverted, plus the checksum, differ from 0xFF), LPERR (identifier parity bits do not match; the hardware does not correct it, software decides), LSERR (SYNCH edges outside tolerance), LFERR (dominant stop bit; also in UART mode), LTOERR (frame not finished within TFrame_Maximum), LOVERR (a command other than abort given while busy; in UART mode, a received byte overwrote the stored one) and LABORT (an abort given while busy). After any LIN error the controller returns to its resting state (LCMD[2..0] = 000). Writing 1 to LERR clears it and all of LINERR.
A time-out error is flagged when a frame takes longer than TFrame_Maximum, which is 1.4 times the nominal header time plus 1.4 times the nominal response time.

A BREAK/SYNC sequence is detected even when the break overlaps a response byte; the current transfer stops and the new frame is handled. A slave flags an error (LBERR in a Tx response, LFERR in an Rx response). A master's software aborts the frame itself with LIN abort followed by Tx header, which sets LABORT. In a slave the break is detected with the timing of the aborted response and resynchronisation then proceeds normally, so time-out values can be slightly off.

The four LINSIR flags drive two interrupts: LIN IT from LIDOK, LTXOK and LRXOK, and LIN ERR from LERR, each flag enabled in LINENIR (LENIDOK, LENTXOK, LENRXOK, LENERR). Identifier filtering is not done in hardware; LINSIR only reports headers with identifiers 0x3C to 0x3F. Frame identifiers 60 (0x3C) and 61 (0x3D) always use the classic checksum, and software switches LIN13 to give that checksum; whether the identifier enters the checksum is fixed just after the Rx or Tx response command starts.

In LIN mode the response data sit in an 8-byte FIFO reached through LINDAT, the index LINDX[2..0] in LINSEL pointing at the byte. With LAINC cleared the index increments after each LINDAT access and wraps from 7 to 0; with LAINC set the index is written before each access. The first byte of a frame is at index 0. LINSEL is set up by software before use. In UART mode LINDAT is a plain data register (written for output, read for input) and LINSEL is unused.

When stopped by the on-chip debugger: LINCR[6..0] are read/write and LSWRES still self-clears; LIDST and LBUSY are readable; LERR and the LxxOK bits are written directly (clearing LERR clears every LINERR bit, setting it sets them all); LINENR, LINERR, LINBRRH/L, LINDLR, LINSEL and LINDAT are fully read/write; LBT[5..0] can be written only with LDISR set; LID[5..0] are read/write and LP[1..0] read-only and updated live; LAINC has no effect and the FIFO is reached by writing LINDX. A debugger break stops the controller's state machine (frame time-out included) and later communication may be corrupted.

A 10-bit successive approximation ADC with 0.5 LSB integral non-linearity and ±2 LSB absolute accuracy, 8 µs to 250 µs conversion time and up to 120 kSPS at full resolution. Its 15-channel multiplexer gives 11 single-ended inputs referred to GND, and three differential amplifiers with gains of 5, 10, 20 and 40 (14 dB, 20 dB, 26 dB, 32 dB, accurate to 5%); about 8-bit resolution is to be expected on amplified channels. The input range is 0 to VCC, the result can be left adjusted, and the reference is AVCC, the internal 2.56 V or the AREF pin. It has free running and single conversion, auto triggering from interrupt sources, a conversion complete interrupt, a sleep-mode noise canceler, a temperature sensor, measurement of the current source voltage (LIN address sense) and of VCC (VCC/4 input). AVCC must stay within ±0.3 V of VCC. PRR.PRADC must be 0 for the ADC to run.

Code 0 is GND and the top code is AREF minus 1 LSB. REFS1:0 in ADMUX connects AVCC or the internal 2.56 V to AREF, whether or not the ADC is enabled; the internal reference is decoupled with a capacitor at AREF. MUX selects any ADC pin, GND or the bandgap reference. ADEN in ADCSRA enables the ADC, which draws no power when ADEN is 0; switching it off before power-saving sleep modes is recommended. The result is right adjusted in ADCH:ADCL, or left adjusted with ADLAR, when reading ADCH alone gives 8 bits. ADCL is read first: reading it blocks updates until ADCH is read, so a conversion that completes in between is lost, though its interrupt still fires.

With PRR.PRADC at 0, writing 1 to ADSC starts a single conversion; ADSC reads 1 until it completes. A channel change during a conversion takes effect after it. ADATE enables auto triggering from the source chosen by ADTS in ADCSRB: a rising edge on the trigger resets the prescaler and starts a conversion, giving fixed intervals. A trigger still high at the end of a conversion does not start another, and edges during a conversion are ignored. The trigger's interrupt flag is set even with the interrupt disabled, and must be cleared before the next event can trigger. Using ADIF itself as the trigger gives free running mode, started by writing ADSC once, with conversions following whether or not ADIF is cleared; free running is not allowed on amplified channels. With auto triggering on, ADSC still starts single conversions and shows a conversion in progress.

The converter needs a clock of 50 kHz to 2 MHz for full resolution; a faster clock gives more samples per second at lower resolution. A 7-bit prescaler (CK/2 to CK/128, set by ADPS in ADCSRA) makes the ADC clock from any CPU clock above 100 kHz; it runs while ADEN = 1 and is held reset while ADEN = 0. A conversion started by ADSC begins on the next rising ADC clock edge. A normal conversion takes 13 ADC clocks, the first after enabling 25, to initialise the analog circuits. Sample-and-hold falls 3.5 clocks into a normal conversion and 13.5 into a first conversion. At completion the result is written, ADIF is set and, in single conversion mode, ADSC clears. With auto triggering the prescaler is reset on the trigger, sample-and-hold comes two ADC clocks after the trigger edge, and three more CPU clocks go to synchronisation. In free running mode the next conversion starts at once, ADSC staying high. After selecting the bandgap as input, the first result may be wrong until the voltage settles.

MUX and REFS are buffered in a temporary register; the selection follows writes until a conversion starts, is then locked, and follows again from the last ADC clock before completion (ADIF set). New values should be written no sooner than one ADC clock after ADSC. With ADATE and ADEN both set an event can come at any time, so ADMUX is safely changed only with ADATE or ADEN cleared, at least one ADC clock after a trigger during a conversion, or after a conversion before the trigger's flag is cleared; the change then applies to the next conversion. After selecting a differential channel, or after changing the reference before a differential conversion, the gain stage needs up to 125 µs to settle, and conversions in that time should not be started or should be discarded. In single conversion mode select the channel before starting (or one ADC clock after ADSC). In free running mode select it before the first conversion; a change after the first conversion shows one result late. Amplified conversions clear ADSC at the end, so free running needs ADSC set again by software after each one. Writing new channel or reference values during free running is not advised. The first result on a differential channel may be poor while the automatic offset cancellation settles and is best discarded.

VREF sets the conversion range; single-ended inputs above VREF read close to 0x3FF. VREF is AVCC (through a passive switch), the internal 2.56 V (from the bandgap VBG through an amplifier) or an external voltage on AREF. AREF connects straight to the ADC, so a capacitor from AREF to ground reduces noise, and VREF can be measured there with a high-impedance meter; VREF is a high-impedance node and should see nothing but capacitance. With a fixed external voltage on AREF the other reference options are not used, since they would be shorted to it; with nothing on AREF the reference can be switched between AVCC and 2.56 V. The first result after switching reference may be inaccurate and should be discarded. AREF is shared with the ISRC current source output; with the current source selected AREF is cut from the internal reference network (AREFEN, ISRCEN in ADCSRB). For differential channels the reference keeps the distance from AVCC that the ADC characteristics require.
