Conversions can run in ADC Noise Reduction or Idle sleep to keep CPU and I/O noise out: with the ADC enabled and idle, single conversion mode and the conversion complete interrupt enabled, entering the sleep mode starts a conversion once the CPU halts. If nothing else wakes the CPU first, the ADC interrupt wakes it; if another interrupt does, it runs and the ADC interrupt follows at completion, the CPU staying awake until the next SLEEP. Other sleep modes do not switch the ADC off, so ADEN should be cleared before them.

Each ADC pin carries its pin capacitance and leakage whether selected or not. When selected, the source charges the 14 pF sample-and-hold capacitor through 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ of series resistance. The ADC is optimised for sources of about 10 kΩ or less, for which sampling time is negligible; higher impedances need longer, variable sampling time, and slowly varying signals suit them. Components above the Nyquist frequency (fADC/2) should be removed with a low-pass filter before the input.

Keep analog tracks short, over the ground plane and away from fast digital tracks. Feed AVCC from VCC through an LC network. Use the noise canceler. Do not switch ADC port pins used as digital outputs during a conversion.

The gain stage nulls most of the differential offset itself. The remaining offset is measured by selecting the same pin for both differential inputs and subtracted in software, which brings the offset on any channel below one LSB.

An n-bit single-ended ADC spans GND to VREF in 2^n steps, codes 0 to 2^n − 1. Offset: how far the first transition (0x000 to 0x001) is from its ideal place at 0.5 LSB; ideal 0 LSB. Gain error: after offset correction, how far the last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) is from its ideal place 1.5 LSB below full scale; ideal 0 LSB. Integral non-linearity: after offset and gain correction, the largest distance of any transition from its ideal place; ideal 0 LSB. Differential non-linearity: the largest difference of a code width from 1 LSB; ideal 0 LSB. Quantisation error: always ±0.5 LSB. Absolute accuracy: the largest distance of any uncorrected transition from ideal, combining all of these; ideal ±0.5 LSB.

ADMUX = 0xED selects ADC3 − ADC2 at 10× gain with the 2.56 V reference and a left adjusted result. With 300 mV on ADC3 and 500 mV on ADC2 the result is 512 × 10 × (300 − 500) / 2560 = −400 = 0x270: ADCL reads 0x00 and ADCH 0x9C. Right adjusted (ADLAR = 0) it reads ADCL = 0x70, ADCH = 0x02.

Writing MUX[4:0] = 10000 selects and enables the on-chip temperature sensor; the internal 2.56 V reference must be selected, and the ADC is used in single conversion mode. The voltage rises about 2.5 mV/°C. After a single calibration at room temperature the accuracy is typically ±10 °C; calibrating at two temperatures does better. The output varies from chip to chip, so each chip needs its own calibration value, kept in EEPROM or a register. Factory calibration values measured hot (about +85 °C) are also in the signature row: TSGAIN, the gain (1, or an unsigned fixed-point number with 0x80 = 1.0), and TSOFFSET, a signed two's complement offset byte.

Three differential amplified channels with gains of 5, 10, 20 and 40. They are switched-capacitor amplifiers clocked by an amplifier synchronisation clock, and the input should be steady for at least four of its periods around the sampling point. The clock, chosen by AMPxTS in AMPxCSR, is CKADC (the ADC clock divided by 8), a Timer0 or Timer1 compare match or overflow, or a PSC event (PSS0, PSS1, PSS2). Synchronised to the ADC clock / 8, a conversion started while CKADC2 is low takes the same 13 ADC clocks as a single-ended one, and 14 if started while it is high. ADMUX selects the amplified channel and ADSC starts the conversion; no other channel can be converted until it finishes. If the amplifier output changes during the ADC sampling phase, the conversion is aborted and restarted once the output is stable. The PSC trigger frequency must stay below ADCclk/4. Auto triggered amplified conversions start on the amplifier clock event after the trigger chosen by ADTS; free running needs ADSC set by software after each conversion. Each amplifier has AMPxEN, AMPxIS, gain AMPxG1:0, AMPCMPx (to route it to an analog comparator) and AMPxTS2:0.

A 100 µA current source with ±2% absolute accuracy, sourced from AVCC out of the AREF/ISRC pin when ISRCEN is set, into an external resistor; otherwise the pin keeps its normal function. The resistor voltage is measured on the ADC input shared with the pin. A series resistor of 0.5% tolerance or better is recommended. The first measurement uses AVCC as the ADC reference to protect against large voltages; another reference can then be chosen from the first result to refine it.

LIN does not say how a node in a cluster gets a unique physical address. An external resistor on the current source sets it: the ADC measures the voltage across the resistor and the value maps to the address the communication handler uses. Because the source is a current, the reading does not depend on the disturbed vehicle supply voltage.

With an external resistor the current source also makes a voltage reference for outside devices, or a threshold for the internal analog comparator on AIN0 (negative input) or AIN1 (positive input). A resistor tolerance tighter than the source's 2% is recommended.

Four fast clocked comparators with ±30 mV hysteresis. Each compares its own positive pin ACMPx with a negative input chosen by ACnM: one of four internal levels derived from the ADC reference (VREF selected by REFS1:0 in ADMUX, divided by 1.60, 2.13, 3.20 or 6.40), the DAC output, or an external pin ACMPMx (ACMPNx). The output ACnO is set when the positive pin is above the negative input. A comparison is made whenever CLKI/O (or CLKI/O/2) falls, chosen by ACCKDIV in ACSR. Each comparator has its own interrupt, triggered on output rise, fall or toggle (ACnIS1:0), and its flags can also synchronise ADC or DAC conversions. Comparator 1's output can trigger the Timer/Counter1 input capture (AC1ICE).
AMPCMP0, AMPCMP1 and AMPCMP2 connect the positive input of comparator 0, 1 or 2 to the output of amplifier 0, 1 or 2; the comparator is then clocked with that amplifier's clock.

A 10-bit DAC with 8-bit linearity and ±0.5 LSB accuracy between 100 mV and AVCC − 100 mV. It can serve as the comparators' negative input, drive the D2A pin, or both, the pin being driven through a dedicated output driver of about 100 Ω output impedance, which can drive 1 nF in parallel with more than 33 kΩ with a time constant of about 1 µs. It uses the separate analog supply AVCC, which must stay within ±0.3 V of VCC, and the same reference as the ADC (the on-chip 2.56 V or AVCC, or AREF), which can be decoupled at the AREF pin.

The output is proportional to the DACH:DACL value, which can be updated by trigger events for accurate sample timing. DACON configures the DAC: once DAEN is set it converts the DACH:DACL value. With DAATE set, a rising edge on the source chosen by DATS starts a conversion; a trigger still high at the end does not start another, edges during a conversion are ignored, and the trigger's flag must be cleared before the next event triggers. DAOE enables the output driver and DALA left-adjusts the value.

VREF sets the DAC range: AVCC through a passive switch, the internal 2.56 V from the bandgap through an amplifier, or an external voltage on AREF, which connects straight to the DAC. A capacitor from AREF to ground reduces noise; AREF, a high-impedance node, takes capacitance only. With a fixed external voltage on AREF the other options are not used; with nothing on AREF the reference can be switched between AVCC and 2.56 V. The first conversion after a reference change may be inaccurate and should be discarded.

A one-wire on-chip debug system: program flow control, emulation of every on-chip function, digital and analog, except the RESET pin, real-time and non-intrusive operation, symbolic debugging, unlimited software break points, and programming of the non-volatile memories. With the DWEN fuse programmed (0) and the lock bits unprogrammed (1), the RESET pin becomes an open-drain bidirectional line with pull-up, the link to the emulator. The system clock stays the source chosen by CKSEL.

A pull-up on dW/RESET must be no smaller than 10 kΩ and is not required. RESET tied directly to VCC does not work. Capacitors on RESET must be removed and all external reset sources disconnected; an external reset is not supported while debugWIRE is on. Break points are BREAK instructions written into flash, each change reprogramming the flash, which shortens flash data retention; parts used for debugging should not be shipped. A programmed DWEN keeps parts of the clock system running in every sleep mode and raises sleep current, so DWEN should be unprogrammed when debugWIRE is not in use.

Read-while-write self-programming lets a flash-resident boot loader load and store program code over any interface. Boot loader code can write the whole flash, itself included, and can erase itself. The boot section size is set by fuses, a separate fuse picks the reset vector, and two independent sets of boot lock bits set the protection. Flash is programmed in pages of several bytes; paging does not affect normal operation.

BOOTSZ fuses split the flash into an application section and a boot loader section (BLS), each with its own lock bits (boot lock bits 0 and 1). SPM can start programming only when executed from the BLS, and can then reach the whole flash; from the application section SPM is disabled.

Independently of BOOTSZ, the flash is split at a fixed point into a read-while-write (RWW) and a no-read-while-write (NRWW) section. Erasing or writing a page in the RWW section leaves the NRWW section readable; erasing or writing a page in the NRWW section halts the CPU for the whole operation. Code in the RWW section can never be read during self-programming: interrupts should be disabled or moved to the BLS, which always lies in the NRWW section. RWWSB in SPMCSR reads 1 while the RWW section is blocked and is cleared by software (RWWSRE) after programming before RWW code is read.

Without a boot loader the whole flash holds application code. The boot lock bits can protect the whole flash, only the BLS, only the application section, or nothing from software update. They are set by software or by serial or parallel programming and cleared only by chip erase. The general lock modes 1 and 2 do not control SPM writes or LPM/SPM reads.

The application enters the boot loader by a jump or call, for example on a command received over USART or SPI. Alternatively the BOOTRST fuse points the reset vector at the boot section start, so the boot loader runs after every reset. The MCU cannot change its own fuses: once BOOTRST is programmed it changes only through serial or parallel programming.

SPM commands are addressed by the Z-pointer (ZH:ZL in the register file, plus RAMPZ in I/O space, which exists only when program space is above 64 Kbytes); the bits used depend on the device. The low bits of the program counter address the word within a page (PCWORD) and the high bits select which page (PCPAGE). Page erase and page write are addressed separately and must address the same page. Once an operation starts the address is latched and Z is free. Setting the boot lock bits ignores Z. LPM addresses bytes, so it also uses Z0.

Flash is written page by page; a page is erased before it is written from the temporary page buffer, which is filled one word at a time with SPM, either before a page erase (allowing read-modify-write of the old page) or between erase and write. Unchanged parts of a page are kept in the buffer and written back. Page erase: Z holds a page number (PCPAGE), SPMCSR is loaded with 0x0000011 and SPM must follow within four clock cycles; R1:R0 are ignored. Page load: Z holds the address, R1:R0 the word, SPMCSR takes 0x00000001, SPM follows within four cycles; PCWORD selects the buffer word. The buffer auto-erases after a page write, on writing RWWSRE or on reset, and each address can be written only once before it is erased; an EEPROM write during page loading loses the loaded data. Page write: Z holds a page number (PCPAGE, other Z bits zero), SPMCSR takes 0x0000101, and SPM follows within four cycles. In each case an RWW-section page leaves the NRWW section readable and an NRWW-section page halts the CPU.

The SPM ready interrupt fires continuously while SPMEN is cleared, replacing polling; the interrupt vectors should then be moved to the BLS so no interrupt reaches the blocked RWW section. Leaving boot lock bit 11 unprogrammed lets the boot loader be overwritten by accident; programming it is recommended when the boot loader itself need not change. During self-programming the RWW section is blocked for reading: software keeps away from it, moves the vectors or disables interrupts, and clears RWWSB by writing RWWSRE before using it again.

operation.topic: Setting and reading lock and fuse bits by software
operation.text: Boot lock and general lock bits are set by writing the bits to R0 (bit 5 BLB12, 4 BLB11, 3 BLB02, 2 BLB01, 1 LB2, 0 LB1; bits 7 and 6 written 1), loading SPMCSR with 0x0001001 and following with SPM inside four cycles; a cleared bit programs that lock. Z is ignored but loading 0x0001 is recommended. The whole flash stays readable meanwhile. An EEPROM write blocks all software flash programming and reading of fuses and locks, so EEPE should be checked clear before writing SPMCSR. To read, set BLBSET and SPMEN in SPMCSR and execute LPM within three cycles with Z = 0x0001 for the lock bits, 0x0000 for the fuse low byte, 0x0003 for the fuse high byte or 0x0002 for the extended fuse byte (bits 3:0). The bits clear after the read or if no LPM follows within three cycles (or no SPM within four). Programmed bits read 0, unprogrammed 1.

operation.topic: Reading the signature row by software
operation.text: Set SIGRD and SPMEN in SPMCSR and execute LPM within three cycles with Z set to the signature byte address; the byte is loaded into the destination register. The bits clear after the read or after three cycles without LPM.

At low VCC the flash can be corrupted, because a write needs a minimum voltage and the CPU can execute instructions wrongly. Any one of these prevents it: program the boot lock bits when the boot loader need not be updated; hold RESET active while the supply is too low, using the brown-out detector if its level fits or an external low-VCC reset otherwise (a write in progress completes if the voltage is enough); or keep the core in power-down sleep during low VCC.

The example routine runs from the boot section (at least its SPM subroutine, since only NRWW code can be read during page erase and write), with interrupts disabled or moved to the boot section. It erases a page, re-enables the RWW section, loads the buffer word by word from RAM, writes that page, re-enables RWW, optionally reads it back to compare, and before returning waits until RWWSB is clear. Its SPM subroutine waits for any previous SPM to finish, saves SREG and disables interrupts, waits for any EEPROM write to finish, writes SPMCSR and executes SPM, then restores SREG.
Six lock bits, unprogrammed (1) or programmed (0), add the protection below; they return to 1 only through chip erase. Fuse bits and boot lock bits are programmed before LB1 and LB2.

Three fuse bytes; a programmed fuse reads 0. Chip erase does not change the fuses. Fuses are locked once LB1 is programmed, so they are programmed before the lock bits. Fuse values are latched on entering programming mode and take effect only on leaving it, except EESAVE, which acts as soon as it is programmed; they are also latched at power-up in normal mode.

The extended fuses PSCRB, PSCARV (PSCRVA) and PSCBRV (PSCRVB) set the PSC output state during reset, to protect external power parts. With PSCRB unprogrammed the PSC outputs behave as normal port pins. With PSCRB programmed they are forced at reset, and stay forced until POC is written: PSCARV programmed forces PSCOUT0A, PSCOUT1A and PSCOUT2A high, unprogrammed forces them low; PSCBRV does the same for PSCOUT0B, PSCOUT1B and PSCOUT2B.

A three-byte signature, readable in serial and parallel mode even when the part is locked, sits in its own address space. A calibration byte for the internal RC oscillator sits in the high byte of address 0x000 of the signature space and is copied into OSCCAL at reset.

Parallel (high-voltage) programming writes and verifies flash, EEPROM, lock bits and fuses. Pulses are at least 250 ns unless stated otherwise. A positive pulse on XTAL1 performs the action coded on XA1:XA0; a pulse on WR or OE performs the loaded command. VCC is 4.5 V to 5.5 V and AVCC within 0.3 V of VCC, itself within 4.5 V to 5.5 V.

Set the Prog_enable pins (PAGEL, XA1, XA0, BS1) to 0000, RESET to 0 V and VCC to 0 V. Apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V between VCC and GND, VCC reaching at least 1.8 V within 20 µs. After 20 µs to 60 µs apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to RESET. Keep the Prog_enable pins steady 10 µs or more once RESET is at high voltage so the signature latches, and wait at least 300 µs before the first command. If VCC cannot rise that fast: apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V, apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to RESET as soon as VCC reaches 0.9 V to 1.1 V, hold Prog_enable for 10 µs, and wait until VCC reaches 4.5 V to 5.5 V before any command. Programming mode ends on power-down or with RESET taken to 0 V.

Command and address are kept between operations: a command is loaded once for many locations, 0xFF need not be written after a chip erase (the whole EEPROM unless EESAVE is programmed, and the flash), and the address high byte is loaded only when moving to a new 256-word flash window or 256-byte EEPROM window (also for signature reads).

Chip erase clears flash, SRAM, EEPROM (unless EESAVE is programmed) and the lock bits, the locks only after the flash is fully erased; fuses are unchanged. It is required before reprogramming flash or EEPROM. Sequence: XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, DATA = 1000 0000, pulse XTAL1 to load the command, pulse WR low to start (RDY/BSY goes low), and wait for RDY/BSY high.

Flash is written a page at a time through a page buffer. A: load command 0001 0000 (XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, pulse XTAL1). B: load the address low byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 0). C: load the data low byte (XA1:XA0 = 01). D: load the data high byte (BS1 = 1, XA1:XA0 = 01). E: latch the data with BS1 = 1 and a positive PAGEL pulse. F: repeat B to E until the buffer is full; the low address bits pick the word in a page and the high bits which page (with fewer than 256 words per page the top bits of the low byte form part of a page number). G: load the address high byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 1). H: pulse WR low to program that page and wait for RDY/BSY high. I: repeat B to H for the whole flash. J: load the no-operation command 0000 0000 to reset the internal write signals.

EEPROM is written a page at a time: load command 0001 0001, address high byte, address low byte, data, latch with PAGEL; repeat address low, data and latch until the buffer is full; then with BS1 = 0 pulse WR low and wait for RDY/BSY high. Reading flash: command 0000 0010, address high and low bytes, then OE = 0 with BS1 = 0 gives the low byte and BS1 = 1 the high byte; OE back to 1. Reading EEPROM: command 0000 0011, address high and low, OE = 0 with BS1 = 0 gives the byte.

All fuse writes load command 0100 0000 and then the data low byte (a 0 bit programs the fuse, a 1 erases it), then pulse WR low and wait for RDY/BSY: with BS1 = 0, BS2 = 0 for the low byte; BS1 = 1, BS2 = 0 for the high byte; BS1 = 0, BS2 = 1 for the extended byte (BS1 and BS2 are then returned to 0). Lock bits: command 0010 0000, data low byte (0 programs the lock), WR pulse; with LB mode 3 the boot lock bits can no longer be programmed externally. Lock bits clear only by chip erase. Reading: command 0000 0100, then with OE = 0, BS2:BS1 = 00 gives the fuse low byte, 11 the fuse high byte, 10 the extended fuse byte and 01 the lock bits (0 means programmed). Signature: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00 to 0x02, OE = 0, BS1 = 0. Calibration byte: command 0000 1000, address low byte 0x00, OE = 0, BS1 = 1.

Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over the SPI bus (SCK, MOSI in, MISO out) while RESET is held at GND; the Programming Enable instruction comes first. VCC is 1.8 V to 5.5 V and AVCC within 0.3 V of VCC, itself within 1.8 V to 5.5 V. A clock is needed as the CKSEL fuses select; with the internal oscillator nothing is connected to XTAL1. EEPROM writes erase each location automatically in serial mode, so chip erase is not needed first; chip erase sets every flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF. SCK low and high times are each more than 2 CPU clocks for fck below 12 MHz and 3 CPU clocks for fck of 12 MHz and above.

Data in are clocked on the rising edge of SCK, data out on the falling edge. Power up with RESET and SCK at 0 (if SCK cannot be held low, give RESET a positive pulse of at least two CPU clocks after SCK is 0). Wait at least 20 ms, then send Programming Enable on MOSI; in sync, the second byte (0x53) echoes back while the third is sent. All four bytes are always sent; without the echo, pulse RESET and retry. Flash is loaded a page at a time, one byte per Load Program Memory Page instruction with the 6 LSB of the address, the low byte before the high byte for each address, then stored with Write Program Memory Page and the 7 MSB of the address; without RDY/BSY polling wait at least tWD_FLASH before the next page. EEPROM is written a byte at a time with the Write instruction (each location auto-erased; wait tWD_EEPROM without polling), or a page at a time with Load EEPROM Memory Page and Write EEPROM Memory Page, which changes only the locations loaded. 0xFF need not be written to an erased part. Any location is verified with a Read instruction on MISO. At the end RESET is set high to run normally; to power off, set RESET to 1 and remove VCC. A 1 in the LSB of the Poll RDY/BSY result means an operation is still pending.

Load instructions put one byte into the buffer at an offset given by the low address bits; the write page instruction then stores the buffer into whichever page the high address bits select, for program memory and EEPROM alike. On the serial interface MOSI and MISO carry each byte MSB first.
The highest clock frequency depends on VCC: 8 MHz at 2.7 V, rising linearly to 16 MHz at 4.5 V, and 16 MHz from 4.5 V up to 5.5 V.

Master mode: 6 runs from SS low to the first SCK edge; 4 and 5 are MISO setup and hold at the sampling edge; 7 runs from an SCK edge to MOSI changing and 8 from the last SCK edge to MOSI's final change; 1 is the SCK period, 2 its high and low times and 3 its rise and fall. Slave mode: 9 runs from SS low to MISO driven; 13 and 14 are MOSI setup and hold; 15 runs from an SCK edge to MISO changing; 10, 11 and 12 are the SCK period, its high and low times and its rise and fall; 16 runs from the last SCK edge to SS high and 17 from SS high to MISO going to tri-state. Both modes hold for CPOL = 0 and CPOL = 1, MSB first.

DATA, XA0/1, BS1 and BS2 are set up tDVXH before XTAL1 rises and held tXLDX after it falls, with XTAL1 high for at least tXHXL. In a write, WR falls tXLWL after XTAL1 low and stays low for tWLWH; RDY/BSY goes low within tWLRL of WR falling and returns high after tWLRH (tWLRH_CE for chip erase). Loading a page takes an address low byte, a data low byte and a data high byte (BS1 high), followed by a PAGEL pulse, spaced by tXLXH, tXLPH and tPLXH. Reading within a page: after the address is loaded, OE low puts the data low byte on DATA within tOLDV, BS1 high switches to the high byte within tBVDV, and OE high releases DATA within tOHDZ. The XTAL1 setup, pulse-width and hold limits apply to loading and reading as well.
